# Importing the Data {#sec-import}

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_common.R")
raw_file <- "../data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT"
if (!file.exists(raw_file)) {
  stop(
    "Cannot find ",
    raw_file,
    ". Run the download chunk in this chapter first (see README)."
  )
}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  cache.extra = c(cache_context, list(data = tools::md5sum(raw_file)))
)
```

## The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System

The [Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/) (BRFSS) is the
largest continuously running health survey in the world. Every year, the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention (CDC) and the states interview hundreds of thousands of US adults by
landline and cell phone about their health conditions, health behaviors, and use of health
care. In 2024, 457,670 adults in 49 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, and
the US Virgin Islands completed the interview (Tennessee did not collect enough data to be
included).

BRFSS is a **complex survey**:

- **Strata.** Each state's sample is drawn separately within strata (for example, by region
  and by landline or cell phone).
- **Primary sampling units (PSUs).** Within a stratum, phone numbers are sampled. In BRFSS
  each respondent is their own PSU.
- **Weights.** People are sampled with different probabilities and respond at different
  rates. CDC's final weight (`_LLCPWT`) corrects for both and makes the weighted sample match
  each state's adult population by age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and other
  characteristics ("raking").

Every estimate in this book uses all three. @sec-descriptives shows what happens when they
are ignored.

## Download the data (run once)

CDC distributes the data as a zipped SAS transport file (`.XPT`), a format that stores a SAS
dataset in a portable way. The zip file is 83 MB, and the unzipped file is 1.1 GB.

Run the chunk below **once**, by hand (it is not run when the book is rendered). It saves
`data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT`. Raw data, processed data and caches are excluded from Git.

```{r}
#| label: download
#| eval: false
dir.create("../data/raw", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
zip_file <- "../data/raw/LLCP2024XPT.zip"
options(timeout = 600) # allow 10 minutes on a slow connection
utils::download.file(
  "https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/files/LLCP2024XPT.zip",
  destfile = zip_file,
  mode = "wb"
)
# The zip file names its contents "LLCP2024.XPT " (with a trailing space), so rename the file.
extracted <- utils::unzip(zip_file, exdir = "../data/raw")
file.rename(extracted, "../data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT")
file.remove(zip_file)
```

::: callout-tip
## Downloading by hand

You can also download the zip file from the
[CDC BRFSS 2024 page](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2024.html) ("2024 BRFSS
Data (SAS Transport Format)"), unzip it, and save the file as `data/raw/LLCP2024.XPT`. The
same page has the codebook, which lists every variable, its question, and its codes.
:::

## Read only the columns we need

The file has 345 columns. We need 13, so we read only those with `col_select`. This keeps
memory use low and makes reading fast. It does not change the survey design: every one of
the 457,670 respondents is kept, with their weight, stratum, and PSU.

| Role | Variables | Codebook label |
|---|---|---|
| Survey design | `_LLCPWT`, `_STSTR`, `_PSU`, `_STATE` | Final weight, stratum, primary sampling unit, state |
| Outcomes | `DIABETE4`, `GENHLTH`, `MEDCOST1` | Ever told you had diabetes; general health; could not afford a doctor |
| Exposure | `INCOME3` | Annual household income |
| Covariates | `_AGE_G`, `SEXVAR`, `_IMPRACE` | Age in six groups; sex; race and ethnicity |
| Auxiliary variables | `EDUCA`, `EMPLOY1` | Education; employment (used only to help impute income in @sec-imputation) |

: The 13 variables used in this book {#tbl-variables}

Names that start with an underscore are variables CDC calculated. In R they must be wrapped
in backticks, as in `` `_LLCPWT` ``.

```{r}
#| label: read
#| cache: true
brfss <- haven::read_xpt(
  raw_file,
  col_select = c(
    `_LLCPWT`,
    `_STSTR`,
    `_PSU`,
    `_STATE`, # survey design
    DIABETE4,
    GENHLTH,
    MEDCOST1, # outcomes
    INCOME3, # exposure
    `_AGE_G`,
    SEXVAR,
    `_IMPRACE`, # covariates
    EDUCA,
    EMPLOY1 # auxiliary variables for imputation
  )
)

# Check: all 457,670 respondents and the 13 columns we asked for.
stopifnot(nrow(brfss) == 457670, ncol(brfss) == 13)
dplyr::glimpse(brfss)
```

Every column is a number: the answers are codes, such as 1 for "Yes" and 7 for "Don't know".
@sec-cleaning turns them into labeled categories.

## Save for the next chapter

Quarto runs each chapter of this book in a fresh R session, so each chapter saves what the
next one needs. An `.rds` file stores one R object exactly as it is in memory.

```{r}
#| label: save
saveRDS(brfss, file.path(processed_dir, "01-brfss.rds"))
```
